To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a series of structually related inhibitors of matrix metaloproteinases were synthesized using protein structure based design, and the compounds were studied in rodent pharmacokinetic, and anti-tumor models.
a series of synthetic matrix metalloproteinase inhibitors were evaluated in a rodent tumor model and one compound, AG3340, showed significant anti-tumor activity against Lewis lung carcinoma.
the pharmacokinetics and anti-tumor efficacies of a series of structually related matrix metalloproteinase inhibitors vary significantly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the discovery of small molecules that are potent inhibitors of matrix metalproteases, and that have good pharmacokinetic properties and are efficacious in vivo.
the discovery of small molecules that inhibit matrix metalloproteinase enzymes and have the potential to be developed into new cancer therapies.
the development of a new class of anti-tumor agents that inhibit matrix metalloproteinase activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the pharmacokinetics of the compounds studied did not correlate with the observed anti-tumor efficacy, and that the efficacy of these compounds against the Lewis lung model was not predictable from their inhibition of the matrix metalloproteinase enzymes.
the pharmacokinetic properties of the compounds studied are not a major contributor to efficacy.
the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of this series of MMP inhibitors are complex and that the relationship between enzyme inhibition and tumor efficacy is not straightforward.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the compounds studied were not generally efficacious, but AG3340, the most potent inhibitor of matrix metalloproteases, showed the most efficacy against the Lewis tumor model.
the pharmacokinetic properties of the compounds are not predictive of their anti-tumor efficacy, and that efficacy is not correlated with enzyme potency.

the compounds tested in this report were generally well tolerated in the mouse and rat and were effective in reducing primary tumor size and the number of metastatic lesions in the Lewis lung carcinoma mouse model.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the pharmacokinetics of these compounds are not a predictor of anti-tumor efficacy, and that efficacy against the Lewis Lung carcinoma model is not a predictor of efficacy against other tumor models, such as the B16 melanoma.

the efficacy of these MMP inhibitors in the Lewis lung model was not correlated with the ability to inhibit the activity of a single MMP, but instead was dependent upon the ability of the compound to inhibit the activity and/or expression of several MMPs in the tumor microenvironment.
it is not possible to predict the in vivo anti-tumor efficacy of matrix metalloprotease inhibitors based on in vitro potency and pharmacokinetics.
